lede: Enzymes are proteins that speed reactions up without being used up. Each has an active site shaped to fit one substrate, which is why you need a different enzyme for starch, protein and fat. Digestion is that idea at work, turning food into molecules small enough to absorb.
can: Label enzyme, substrate, active site and product on a lock and key diagram.
Name what carbohydrase, protease and lipase digest and produce.
Explain why large insoluble food molecules have to be broken down.

text: Enzymes, the lock and key, and digestion

md: An enzyme is a protein with a dent in it shaped to fit one particular molecule. Your gut is full of them, taking food apart fast enough to be absorbed, and the same proteins lift egg and grease out of a shirt at 40 °C.

alt: Three stages. First, a substrate made of two joined parts sits above an enzyme with a notch-shaped active site of the matching shape. Second, the substrate is in the active site, forming the enzyme-substrate complex. Third, the two products have separated and left, and the enzyme is unchanged with its active site empty.

md: An enzyme is a **protein** that acts as a **biological catalyst**: it speeds up the rate of a reaction **without being used up**. That last clause is a marking point of its own — the enzyme is still there at the end, ready for the next molecule, which is why a cell needs so little of it.

prompt: Enzymes are made of which type of molecule?
explain: Protein — which is why heat and pH can wreck them, as you will see in the next topic.

md: **The lock and key model.** The enzyme has a dent in it called the **active site**. The **substrate** — the molecule the enzyme works on — has a shape **complementary** to that active site, so it fits in. While it is there the reaction happens, and the **products** leave. The enzyme is unchanged and does it all again.

prompt: The part of an enzyme that the substrate fits into is called the ______ ______ .
explain: The active site. Both words are needed; 'site' on its own is not credited, and neither is 'the dent'.

title: Why the shape matters so much
md: The fit is what makes the reaction happen, and it is also what makes each enzyme **specific**. If the substrate's shape does not match the active site, nothing happens at all — the enzyme simply ignores it. That is why you need a different enzyme for starch, for protein and for fat, rather than one all-purpose one.

alt: One enzyme with a notch-shaped active site, drawn beside three possible substrate molecules: A has the matching notch shape, B is a rectangle and C is a circle. Only A can fit.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 720 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="e62t"><title id="e62t">One enzyme and three possible substrate molecules, only one of which has a shape complementary to the active site</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M40 200 H160 V126 H132 L120 148 H80 L68 126 H40 Z"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M280 60 H352 L336 102 H296 Z"/><rect x="440" y="60" width="70" height="42" rx="6"/><circle cx="606" cy="81" r="24"/></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-weight="600">One enzyme</text><text x="270" y="30" font-weight="600">Three possible substrates</text><text x="300" y="132">A</text><text x="470" y="132">B</text><text x="600" y="132">C</text><text x="20" y="232">Only A has a shape complementary to this active site, so only A can be broken down by this enzyme.</text><text x="20" y="248" font-size="11.5">That is what substrate specificity means: one enzyme, one job.</text><text x="166" y="150">active site</text></g></svg>
caption: Substrate specificity: only A fits, so only A is broken down.

prompt: Look at the figure. Which molecule is the substrate for this enzyme?
explain: A, because its shape is complementary to the active site. The other two cannot enter, so the enzyme has no effect on them.

alt: A table with three rows. Carbohydrase, also called amylase, works on starch and produces simple sugars such as glucose. Protease works on protein and produces amino acids. Lipase works on fat or lipid and produces fatty acids and glycerol.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="e63t"><title id="e63t">The three digestive enzymes with the substrate each one works on and the products it makes</title><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none"><path d="M20 40 h720 v160 h-720 z"/><path d="M20 78 h720 M20 118 h720 M20 158 h720"/><path d="M260 40 v160 M470 40 v160"/></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor" font-weight="600"><text x="32" y="64">Enzyme</text><text x="272" y="64">Substrate (large, insoluble)</text><text x="482" y="64">Products (small, soluble)</text></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="32" y="104">carbohydrase (amylase)</text><text x="272" y="104">starch</text><text x="482" y="104">simple sugars (glucose)</text><text x="32" y="144">protease</text><text x="272" y="144">protein</text><text x="482" y="144">amino acids</text><text x="32" y="184">lipase</text><text x="272" y="184">fat (lipid)</text><text x="482" y="184">fatty acids and glycerol</text></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="28">Each enzyme is named after the substrate it works on, not the product it makes.</text></g></svg>
caption: Read across, never down: each enzyme keeps its own row.

md: Each one is named after **what it works on**, not what it makes. **Carbohydrase** (the one you meet is **amylase**) digests starch into simple sugars. **Protease** digests protein into amino acids. **Lipase** digests fat into fatty acids and glycerol. Three rows, and the question usually gives you one cell and asks for another.

prompt: Lipase digests fat into glycerol and ______ ______ .
explain: Fatty acids. Both products are wanted, so 'glycerol' alone is half an answer.

title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q5(b)
md: A diagram showed three molecules in a lock and key reaction and asked for **two terms for each one**. Most candidates picked up some of the six marks, but the report says identifying the terms for the three molecules was difficult. The fix is mechanical: for each molecule ask 'what is its **job** here — enzyme, substrate or product?' and then 'what is its **name** — lipase, fat, glycerol?' Two answers, two different kinds of answer.

prompt: Lipase breaks fat into fatty acids and glycerol. Which of the three is the substrate?
explain: Fat. Lipase is the enzyme and glycerol is one of the products.

text: Why digestion needs them at all

alt: A large insoluble molecule drawn as four joined circles is acted on by an enzyme and becomes four separate small soluble molecules, which pass through the gut wall into the blood.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 740 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="e64t"><title id="e64t">A large insoluble molecule digested by an enzyme into small soluble molecules that pass through the gut wall into the blood</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><circle cx="70" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="98" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="126" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="154" cy="120" r="16"/><circle cx="330" cy="102" r="13"/><circle cx="372" cy="132" r="13"/><circle cx="414" cy="100" r="13"/><circle cx="352" cy="168" r="13"/><path d="M520 40 v180" stroke-dasharray="7 5"/><path d="M600 40 v180"/><path d="M600 60 c40 20 40 60 0 80 c-40 20 -40 60 0 80"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"><path d="M188 120 h72" marker-end="url(#ab64)"/><path d="M448 120 h50" marker-end="url(#ab64)"/></g><defs><marker id="ab64" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-weight="600">Digestion</text><text x="20" y="176">large, insoluble</text><text x="20" y="192">molecule</text><text x="196" y="112">enzyme</text><text x="320" y="210">small, soluble</text><text x="320" y="226">molecules</text><text x="480" y="240">gut wall</text><text x="612" y="34">blood</text><text x="20" y="252" font-size="12">Only small soluble molecules can pass through the gut wall and be absorbed into the bloodstream.</text></g></svg>
caption: Large and insoluble on the left; small, soluble and absorbed on the right.

md: Food molecules arrive **large and insoluble** — too big to cross the gut wall. Enzymes break them into **small, soluble** molecules that **can be absorbed into the bloodstream**. Those four adjectives are the answer to 'why is digestion necessary', and CCEA's glossary uses exactly them.

prompt: Why must large food molecules be digested?
options: They are insoluble and too large to be absorbed into the blood
They contain too much energy to be used at once
They would be attacked by bacteria in the gut
answer: They are insoluble and too large to be absorbed into the blood
explain: Size and solubility. The small soluble products can pass through the gut wall; the large insoluble ones cannot.

md: **Outside the body.** Because enzymes work at low temperatures and break big molecules into small ones, industry uses them too. **Biological washing powders** contain protease and lipase, so they lift protein stains such as blood and egg, and grease, at 30 or 40 °C instead of a hot wash. That saves energy and money — the 'commercial and economic uses' the specification asks for.

prompt: Which two enzymes would be most useful in a biological washing powder for egg and grease stains?
explain: Egg is protein, so protease; grease is fat, so lipase. Naming the stain first tells you the enzyme.

md:
Say what an enzyme is: a **protein** that is a **biological catalyst**, not used up.
Use **enzyme, substrate, active site** and **product** on a lock and key diagram.
Name what **carbohydrase, protease** and **lipase** each digest and produce.
Explain why digestion is needed: **large and insoluble** to **small and soluble**.

On the paper every series, six to nine marks, usually with a lock-and-key diagram: the type of molecule an enzyme is, the letter of the substrate, terms matched to molecules, the enzyme for a named food, and why digestion is needed. The listing rule is live on every *give the letter* part, where two letters score nothing. Stuck: keep the answer short.
